questions.question_text: In a maths quiz out of $15$, $5$ students scored $9$, $12$, $8$, $13$ and $10$. Calculate the population standard deviation of the scores, correct to $2$ decimal places.

options.why: Divided the sum of squares by $n-1$ (sample SD) instead of $n$.
Stopped at the variance and never took the square root.
Found the range (max $-$ min) instead of the standard deviation.

questions.question_text: In a general knowledge quiz out of $20$, $4$ students all scored $12$. Calculate the population standard deviation of their scores.

options.why: Gave the mean instead of the standard deviation.
Used the test's total possible marks instead of calculating the spread of the scores.
Added all the values instead of measuring the spread.

questions.solution_text:
$\sigma_x = 0$
All four scores are identical, so there is no spread in the data.

questions.question_text: In a placement test out of $100$, two students scored $15$ and $55$. Calculate the population standard deviation of their scores.

options.why: Divided by $n-1$ (sample SD) instead of $n$.
Found the range instead of the standard deviation.
Gave the mean instead of the standard deviation.

questions.solution_text:
$\sigma_x = 20$
With only two values, $\sigma_x$ is always exactly half the range.

questions.question_text:
Two classes sat the same test, out of $40$ marks, and both averaged the same mean of $25$.
Class A: $22$, $27$, $25$, $26$
Class B: $17$, $33$, $19$, $31$
Which class had the more consistent results?

options.text: Class A, since $\sigma_x \approx 1.87$ for Class A and $\sigma_x \approx 7.07$ for Class B — the smaller standard deviation means less spread.
Class B, since $\sigma_x \approx 7.07$ for Class B and $\sigma_x \approx 1.87$ for Class A — the larger standard deviation means more consistency.
options.why: Reversed the rule, treating a larger standard deviation as more consistent rather than less.

options.text: Neither class is more consistent, because both classes have exactly the same mean mark.
options.why: Assumed equal means implies equal spread, ignoring the standard deviation entirely.

options.text: Class B, since its scores are spread across a wider range of values, showing more consistency in ability.
options.why: Treated a wider spread as a sign of consistency rather than the opposite.

questions.solution_text:
Class A:
$\sigma_x = 1.8708287...$
$\approx 1.87$
Class B:
$\sigma_x = 7.0710678...$
$\approx 7.07$
Class A has the smaller $\sigma_x$, so Class A's results were more consistent.

questions.question_text: Two classes sit the same test. Class X has $\sigma_x = 2.1$ marks and Class Y has $\sigma_x = 5.6$ marks, with very similar means. Which class's marks are more consistent?

options.text: Class X, because a smaller standard deviation means the marks are less spread out.
Class Y, because a bigger standard deviation means the marks are further from zero.
options.why: Confused the standard deviation with the size of the raw scores themselves.

options.text: Class Y, because more spread means a wider range of ability was tested.
options.why: Treated greater spread as a strength rather than reduced consistency.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the individual scores.
options.why: Overlooked that the standard deviation alone is sufficient to compare consistency.

questions.solution_text:
Class X has the smaller standard deviation.
A smaller $\sigma_x$ means the marks sit closer to the mean on average, so Class X's marks are more consistent.
